entries.title: Rename the lyx binary to lyr (name clash with LyX)
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #670](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/670).

`lyx` collides with LyX, the LaTeX editor, which ships as the `lyx` package in Ubuntu/Debian and installs `/usr/bin/lyx`.
On a machine with both, whichever comes first on PATH wins: a shell where `~/go/bin` is not yet on PATH starts the LaTeX editor instead of LoomYard.
LyX is common among researchers, so the clash is likely for other users too.

Operator decision 2026-10-17: rename the binary to `lyr` (LoomYard Runner), replacing the first proposal `lyd`.
Checked 2026-10-17: `lyr` is no Ubuntu package name, is not installed on the operator's machine, and a web search found no CLI tool whose binary is named `lyr`.
Rejected: `warp` and `ply` are Ubuntu packages, `weft` and `warp` are already fabric terms here, and the four-letter weaving names (`pirn`, `sley`) are longer to type.

Scope: the `cmd/lyx` build target and `binaryName()` in `tools/deploy`, docs and README, stencils and skills in the `ly` plugin that invoke `lyx`, and any scripts or launchers that call it.

## Operator decision (2026-10-22)

The rename runs alone, with no other run in flight, since it touches nearly every file; it is promoted and started only then.

## Name reopened (operator, 2026-10-22)

The operator has not settled the new name: `lyd` or `lyr` is open again, so the 2026-10-17 choice of `lyr` no longer stands until the operator decides.

entries.title: [.NET 004] Regression as three Drift rows: Drift-Baseline after Discussion, Drift-Await before Webster, Drift-Verify after the Code perch
entries.brief: Support a hub regression tier that writes profiles on the parent before implementation and compares after, switchable per task for expected drift.
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-17)

The operator's C# work repository has a regression tier: a suite run before the implementation writes profiles, and the same suite run after it compares against them to catch drift.
Many tasks there are pure refactorings that must not change behaviour, and this tier is what proves it.
Operator view, not a decision: regression tests are not always wanted, since some tasks expect drift, for example when a model is changed; this must be handled, perhaps by a flag on the task in the board.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

- A per-task setting in the board entry's `run_settings`, with three values:
  - `off`: no baseline, no compare.
  - `preserve`: any drift fails the final gate, as a verify failure.
  - `expect-drift`: baseline and compare still run, but the drift report goes to the reviewers and the alignment agent, who judge whether it matches the task's goal; drift alone fails nothing.
  The hub's default lives in config.
- The hub declares the tier in `language.yaml` as three commands: the profile generator, the compare (the repository's own tool, with its tolerances) and the profile directory. lyx only orchestrates and knows no format.
- Operator view, not a decision: the baseline belongs in shed as a producer; it often takes long, so it should start at the beginning as an async command while Discussion and the rest run.
- Orch recommendation, not a decision: shed runs one producer at a time today, so async becomes a generic shed pair of ordinary producers, usable by any recipe:
  - `Job-Start` (a side action with a config flag) starts a detached job, records its handle in run state and returns at once.
  - `Job-Join` waits for the job and fails with its log when it failed.
- Operator view, not a decision: the baseline runs in the task worktree itself, since loom changes no code before Webster, and its output goes to a gitignored place such as `.scratch/`; large simulation time series are never committed.
- Operator decision 2026-10-17: `Job-Join` sits right before Webster, the first row that changes code, so Webster never edits or builds (`bin/`, `obj/`) while the baseline still runs; when Discussion and Plan take longer than the baseline, the join costs nothing.
- Operator view, not a decision: fixed rows in loom for a case that may never come feel clumsy, but each only checks its flag and moves on in milliseconds when it is off.
- Precedent: batten's Open-Window, Seed-IDE and Open-IDE are such rows today, each with an `entry_gate` on a `batten.yaml` flag read from the pair's config stack (shed skips the row and follows `on_done` when the gate is false), so a task's `run_settings` sets it per task. Unlike those, `Job-Join` must be able to fail the run, since those rows only warn.
- The job takes a gate slot like every test run, and obeys a hub pause like the run's other work (note `pause-background-work`).
- Batten tears the job down with the run.
- The compare runs at the final gate only, never per card, to keep the cost down.

## Stations (operator view, not a decision, 2026-10-17)

Loom's recipe could hold fixed command boxes of one type, each taking several entries set per repository:

- Before Discussion: a box that starts the async regression suite, which writes the baseline. The IDE and terminal rows may be their own box of the same type; they stay in any case.
- Right before Webster: a box that only waits for the regression suite to finish.
- Before Finalize: a box that checks whether the regression passed. What it does when it did not is the open hard part.

## On a failed compare (orch recommendation, not a decision)

- Place the compare right after the Webster review (before Describe and Merge-In), not before Finalize: the baseline and the code then share one parent, so drift from other tasks landed meanwhile never enters the compare, which settles the parent-move question.
- Operator view, not a decision: a jump back to `Webster-Burler-Review` on a failed compare is jumping around, and not clean.
- `preserve`: the compare is its own perch, built like every other perch: a check row that runs the compare command, and a fix row that gets the drift report as its finding and hands back to the check. It loops under its own caps and escalates to the orch past them, with no jump into another segment.
- Operator view, not a decision (stated as very important): when regression is not needed, all of it is skipped completely.
  Orch recommendation, not a decision: with `off`, or no regression tier in the hub's `language.yaml`, every regression row is a no-show that reads its setting and is Done: no job starts, no slot is taken, no build runs and no agent is spawned; a hub with no regression tier never shows these rows in its status.
- Operator view, not a decision: a perch in loom's main line starts whatever happens, so it is not skipped by itself.
  Orch recommendation, not a decision: skip it the way darn skips its review perch today: the perch's first row carries an `entry_gate` (darn's Describe row has `entry_gate: budget.Code-Review`), so with a budget of 0 shed records a `skipped` entry and follows `on_done` past the perch (see `contracts/recipes/darn-recipe.yaml`). With regression off for the task or the hub, the regression perch's first row gets an `entry_gate` on the setting the same way, and the task's `run_settings` sets it per task.
  The perch's check row runs the compare command, not an LLM judge, so even when it is entered no agent starts until the compare fails.
- Operator view, not a decision: a compare that finds no drift is skipped onward too.
  Orch recommendation, not a decision: under `preserve` the check row passes and the fix row never runs, so no agent is spawned. Under `expect-drift`, no drift is itself worth a line to PR-Align, since a model change that moves no numbers may not have taken effect.
- `expect-drift`: the compare fails nothing; the drift report goes to PR-Align, where the alignment agent judges it against the task's goal and escalates when it cannot tell.

## Open

- How long the generator takes on the work machine, and whether it can be scoped like the other tiers.
- Whether `preserve` should also run the compare per batch, to point at the card that caused drift.
- A parent that moves during the run is merged in at Merge-In, after the baseline was taken: drift from other landed tasks then shows in the compare. Re-take the baseline at the new parent, or accept it as a known limit.

## Operator decision (2026-10-21): asynchronous tiers in shed

The baseline is the hub's asynchronous test tier, declared in the tier config of task `test-tiers`.
Shed gets a row that starts an asynchronous tier in the background and records the job, and a later row that waits for it to finish; the rows between them run as usual.
The pre-implementation capture on the parent (the detached capture under Models baseline harness) runs through the same pair of rows.

## Related

Task `test-tiers` and task `dotnet-scoped-verify`, which took in note `dotnet-verify-protocol` but left its baseline part here.

## Models baseline harness (from note `dotnet-verify-protocol`, issue #609, 2026-10-24)

`NORCE.Models.NumericalBaseline` runs five purpose-built regression programs plus fixtures and string-compares their scrubbed console output against stored files; one run proves nothing.

- **Capture:** `dotnet test NORCE.Models.NumericalBaseline -p:RunBaseline=true --nologo`, run from `src/csharp/NORCE.Models/`. With no baseline present, every fixture reports `Inconclusive` and writes `<Fixture>.<Method>.txt` plus `_source.txt` (commit, branch, dirty flag, timestamp) into the gitignored `.scratch/numerical-baseline/`; baselines are never committed.
- **Verify:** the same command plus `-e NORCE_BASELINE_MODE=verify`. A missing baseline is a hard failure; a deviation fails with the first differing index, the baseline path and the source commit.
- **Side capture for diagnosis:** `-e NORCE_BASELINE_DIR=<absolute dir>` writes the post-change output into a separate directory, to diff fixture by fixture.

What the tool must do:
1. Capture at the branch point, in the task worktree, before the first code change; never from a second checkout (Millhouse #1181). If code has already changed, do not capture: halt.
2. Before reusing a baseline, check that `_source.txt`'s commit is the branch point by `git diff <commit> -- '*.cs'` being empty, not by the dirty flag.
3. Verify at landing in verify mode; a capture-mode `Inconclusive` is never a pass.
4. On deviation, halt for the operator with a per-fixture diff; never auto-fix, never delete or overwrite a baseline. Intended drift is common; a refresh is an explicit operator command that backs up the old directory first.
5. Carry "no drift" or the per-fixture drift summary into the change description.
6. Wanted: per-batch drift snapshots, diagnostic only, never a gate.

Detached capture: it starts at spawn on the spawn HEAD and records that commit; implementation waits for it before the first edit; a failed or timed-out capture halts before implementation and never falls back to a later capture; it has a timeout and a log that survives teardown; it builds with the gate properties and holds no lock that blocks the agent.

## Operator design (2026-10-24): three Drift rows

This section replaces everything above it on how the regression runs: the stations, the compare perch, the Job-Start/Job-Join pair, the per-task `off`/`preserve`/`expect-drift` setting and the tier declaration.

- Regression is not a test tier: no gate runs it, it is never narrowed or carried, it has two commands (capture and compare), and its outcome is a drift report for an agent, not pass or fail.
  It gets its own config block in the module that owns the Drift rows: a hub flag turning it on, the capture command, the compare command, where the drift report goes, how a skip list of tests is passed in, and the models of its agents.
  Its commands still take a gate slot, so it never runs beside other heavy test runs.
- Experience from Models: unwanted small drift is beyond Webster's Sonnet implementer; finding why takes a stronger agent with overview, tracing and logging and many varied test runs.
- Discussion knows nothing of regression; its stencil stays the same for every hub.

Loom gets three rows, each a no-show that spawns nothing when the hub's flag is off:

1. `Drift-Baseline`, after Discussion: a Sonnet agent reads the decision record and decides the task's regression scope: off (the task changes the model on purpose), partial (with the tests that will drift totally, which are not run), or full (a pure refactoring, everything byte-identical), and writes down the drift it expects.
   When regression is on, it starts the baseline capture in the background in the task worktree and moves on, so Plan runs meanwhile.
2. `Drift-Await`, right before Webster: mechanical, no LLM; it waits until the capture is done, since no code may change before the baseline exists.
   Plan takes far longer than the regression suite, so it rarely waits.
   A capture in a separate checkout was rejected: a .NET build in a fresh worktree takes too long.
3. `Drift-Verify`, after Webster and the Code perch, before Describe and Merge-In: runs the compare mechanically; when it passes, no LLM is spawned.
   When it fails, it spawns one strong agent (Opus or stronger, a config setting) that, within a budget, judges which drift is acceptable against the task and `Drift-Baseline`'s expectation, finds the cause of the rest and fixes it until the compare passes; it writes its reasoning down and escalates to the orch when unsure or past its budget.
   One agent does both judging and fixing; it is no perch.

Darn: `Drift-Baseline` runs before Darn-Write, reads the board entry instead of the decision record, and runs the capture to the end before Darn-Write starts, so darn has no `Drift-Await`; `Drift-Verify` runs after Darn-Write and before Code-Review.

Open:

- Most loom users never use these rows, so they should not clutter the recipe or its status: hide skipped Drift rows from status when the hub's flag is off, or add them as a recipe overlay only a hub with regression turns on.
- Whether `Drift-Verify`'s own code changes need a review, since it sits after the Code perch: accept them, or send the run once more through the Code perch when it changed code.
- The drift report's format, pinned in `contracts/specs/`, written by the repository's compare tool.
- The Models side: its regression project writes that report, which is work in the Models repository.
- `carry: false` from `dotnet-scoped-verify` was built with regression in mind; the timing tier still needs it.

entries.title: Parallel batches: the shared pieces for Webster forks and Weaver
entries.brief: DAG batchifier, worktree per batch, merge-back with conflict resolution; open: keeping a fork inside its worktree
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-17)

The pieces parallel batches need are the same whether a batch starts as a Webster fork or as a cold Weaver agent (see `weaver`); only the spawn differs.

1. A DAG batchifier: edges from the cards' targets and `Uses:`, cards joined into batches while the batch graph stays acyclic and under a cost budget, ready batches chosen. New.
2. A worktree per batch, created for the batch and removed after it. New; may build on fabric.
3. Merge-back of each batch worktree into the task branch, with a cheap model such as Haiku resolving textual conflicts. New.
4. The verify on the merged result and its failure ladder. Exists in Webster (verify gate).
5. The batch brackets and report: `begin-batch`, `record-batch`, the changed-files guard and the report contract. Exist in Webster.
6. `plan-dag-view`, to see the graph and the batches. Note filed.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17)

- Start with these pieces, built so both Webster and Weaver can use them; Webster can run parallel forks first.
- The hard part is getting a Webster fork to work in another worktree than its master's.
- Claude Code's own worktree isolation for agents has given the operator only trouble before.

## Open

How a fork is kept inside its batch's worktree: it inherits the master's working directory and a context full of paths into the task worktree, and `lyx` commands find their anchor from the working directory.

### Orch recommendation

Bench before build: a small proof of concept in which one fork is told to work in a worktree Go created, with absolute paths, and a PreToolUse hook refuses its Edit and Write calls outside that worktree, so a slip is refused instead of landing in the wrong tree; measure whether the fork stays inside and what `lyx` commands it needs a directory flag for.

entries.title: [WS 007] An anchor per umbrella
entries.brief: Let a beam work in its own subdirectory of the repository, inherited by its tasks; loom-sized, best with or after umbrella-groundwork
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-18)

The anchor (`fabric clone --subpath`) is set once per hub and decides where `_lyx`, `.lyx/` and config sit in every worktree of the hub.

## Idea

Let an umbrella (`orch-any-worktree`) have an anchor of its own, a different subdirectory of the repository, inherited by every task under it as it inherits the branch.
Fabric, batten and loom would then read the anchor from the task's umbrella rather than from the hub.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-24)

Low priority. Every beam has a parent, so a beam could get an anchor different from its parent's, which gets messy: at landing, the beam's `_lyx/` files, decisions and config would sit under a different subdirectory than the parent reads.
One way out (orch suggestion, not decided): only a beam directly under `main` may have its own anchor; a sub-beam always inherits its parent's.

## Effort study (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-24)

Medium-hard, loom-sized, not a darn.
- The read side is central: `lyxcwd.resolveCore` alone reads the hub marker `_board/.lyx-anchor`, and the anchor travels as `Location.AnchorRel` (about 50 non-test uses in about 25 packages).
- Hub-wide assumptions are scattered: `fabricengine/warplayout.go` copies the prime's anchor to siblings, as do `pairteardown/teardown.go` and `fabricengine/forkrecords.go`; weft pathspecs, `_portals/`, `_launchers/` and the hub workspace file are keyed on one anchor; `fabricengine/codebinding.go` reads the marker itself.
- Hardest design point: the beam's anchor cannot live in its origin record under `<anchor>/_lyx/`, since the anchor is needed to find it; it needs an anchor-independent index on Bolt.
- Size: 6-8 packages in substance, about 600-1000 lines of code and 400-800 of tests; safer split into lookup and `Location` plumbing, then pair and weft pathspecs, then portals, launchers and workspace.
- Cheapest together with or just after `umbrella-groundwork`, which changes the same seams (`add.go`, `origin.go`, `warplayout.go`, teardown).

## Why an anchor per worktree (operator, 2026-10-24)

The anchor decides where the weft junctions are made and placed inside the matching warp, and where the hub's and each beam's VS Code workspace file roots a worktree; both let work happen in a deep subdirectory without walking far down to it.
All beams share one hub and one board, so a separate hub per subdirectory (`fabric clone --subpath`, a whole new weft repo and board) is no answer.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-24): `.lyx-anchor` at each weft branch's root

- Every weft branch may carry a `.lyx-anchor` at its own root, so the anchor is set per beam and in effect per worktree.
- This breaks the circular lookup above: the weft worktree sits at `<hub>/<slug>-weft`, so lyx finds the marker without knowing the anchor.
- Inheritance comes from git: a task's weft branch starts from its beam's weft branch and carries the beam's marker; a worktree with another anchor commits its own.
- No marker stays on Bolt: `fabric clone --subpath` writes the first `.lyx-anchor` at the root of `main-weft`, and every weft branch starts from there, so every worktree has one; `lyxcwd.resolveCore` reads the worktree's own marker, and everything that reads `Location.AnchorRel` follows.
- The work is in the code that builds another worktree's paths from its own anchor (`warplayout.go`, `teardown.go`, `forkrecords.go`), `codebinding.go`'s own marker read, and the one-anchor keys of `_portals/`, `_launchers/` and the workspace files: each must resolve that worktree's own anchor.
- Changing a worktree's anchor becomes a modest verb: remove its weft junctions, move its files in the weft to the new anchor and commit the new marker, recreate the junctions at the new place in the warp, and regenerate the workspace files that list it.
  Moving the files covers the warp's machine-local `<anchor>/.lyx/` as well.
  No run may be in flight in the worktree while it moves (operator, 2026-10-24).
  Operator view, not a decision: changing the anchor of a worktree that already has child worktrees is very messy, since the children keep the old one.
- Creating a beam takes a simple option for a new anchor (such as `lyx beam create --anchor <dir>`); the default is the anchor of the worktree it is spawned from, which becomes its parent (operator, 2026-10-24).
- To check: if a weft branch merges into its parent's weft at landing, the parent keeps its own `.lyx-anchor`, kept out of the merge as raddle is.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-24): one large isolated task

The operator is very sceptical that this works.
When it becomes a task, it is one large, isolated task that preferably runs alone, closely watched, and is rolled back through git if it goes wrong.

entries.title: Recurring test-suite time and growth audit
entries.brief: Re-run cmd/testtiming against test-suite-timing.md to watch suite growth
entries.body:
## What this is

A recurring audit of test-suite growth, run with `go run ./cmd/testtiming` (Tier 1) and `go run ./cmd/testtiming -full` (Tier 2), and compared against the latest after-state in `docs/benchmarks/test-suite-timing.md`.
It replaces the per-package test-count budget that `test-budget-remove` deleted (operator decision 2026-10-17): count is kept down in review by `PATTERN-test-speed`, which absorbed `PATTERN-test-economy` in `04aafa88c`, and this audit watches the wall time and the per-package test counts that review cannot see in aggregate.
Each audit appends its numbers as a new section of `docs/benchmarks/test-suite-timing.md`, under the method that file states.

## What to look at

- Wall time per tier against the previous section, and the packages that moved most.
- Per-package test counts from `cmd/testtiming`'s `TESTS` column, and which packages grew since the previous audit.
- A growth with no matching new behavior is a candidate for a prune task under `PATTERN-test-speed`.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

Run the audit every two weeks or after about 50 landed tasks, whichever comes first.
A cheap model (Sonnet) runs the measurement; the orch writes the section and files a prune task when a package grew without cause.

entries.title: [WS 005] One dobby daemon per beam owns and drives its runs
entries.brief: Each beam (a worktree with an orch thread) gets a Go daemon, started by lyx orch start, that follows its runs status files, starts ready tasks, lands, settles mechanical stops and tells the thread only what needs judgement
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-18)

- Every batten run is its own Go process in a tmux window, and its Run-Shed row waits on the child with no time limit (`internal/battenshed/doc.go`): it sends halt notices, retries the first verify failure, revives a dead driver's strands, and lands and tears down once the child is done.
- Nothing restarts those processes after a machine restart; `lyx batten run <slug>` resumes from disk, and each row is idempotent, but someone must run it.
- The orch already has a Go daemon of its own, the watcher (`lyx orch watch`).

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-18)

An orchestrator gets not only a long-lived thread but a daemon that looks after every batten run it owns (those whose parent is its worktree) and sets their next steps going; see `orch-split`.

## Agreed in discussion (2026-10-18)

- One daemon per umbrella (see `orch-any-worktree`), the orch watcher, replaces one waiting batten process per run.
- The daemon follows its runs' status files (fsnotify, with a periodic re-read as a fallback where file watching is unreliable, such as WSL and junctions); the child only writes its status, as today, and knows nothing of its owner.
- Creel only where an agent must be told: the daemon posts to its thread when something needs judgement.
- The same pass finds dead drivers, so after a restart only the daemons need starting, one per umbrella.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

1. Step 1: the Run-Shed row checks the child once and exits while it still runs; the daemon re-runs `lyx batten run <slug>` for each run it owns, so notices, the verify retry, revival and landing stay batten's own code, run in short passes.
2. Step 2, optional and later: move logic from batten into the daemon.

Open: who owns a run whose parent has no running daemon, the same problem as a thread that is not running.

## Operator decisions (2026-10-18, later)

- Everything `orch-split` proposed at the hub level belongs here: a Go program in each beam drives the runs of that beam, so the thread the operator talks to gets only what needs judgement; the split into two LLM agents is settled by the daemon, with no second LLM.
  Its later steps: start ready tasks with their run settings, run the landing routine, settle mechanical stops by rule with a cold helper where no rule fits, and the landing check for per-worktree config below.
- A worktree must be settable as a beam, the worktree with a thread and a daemon (see `orch-any-worktree` for the create command and the convert verb); the word replaces "umbrella" for that worktree, while the group of tasks is the project.
- The daemon never starts with the machine: `lyx orch start`, with or without `--continue`, starts the daemons of every beam in the hub, which after a restart replaces running `lyx batten run <slug>` for each run in flight.
- The daemon outgrows the name `ORCHWATCH` (its name and creel sender are now set below).

## Operator decisions (2026-10-18, beam and orch apart)

These replace the earlier wording above where they differ: the daemon is not the orch watcher, and `lyx orch start` does not own the daemons.

- A beam is a worktree plus its Go daemon, and is its own module, `lyx beam`.
  The daemon starts ready tasks, follows their batten runs, lands them and cleans up; it holds no LLM.
- An orch is only an LLM with a role: interactive and long-lived, hence its own watcher for context cycling.
  An orch can be attached to a beam, but a beam runs its tasks with no orch at all.
- What a beam's daemon cannot settle escalates upward: through the arbiter first, then to the beam's orch, or, when the beam has none, to the parent beam's orch, up to the prime.
- `lyx beam start` starts the daemons of every beam in the hub, and `lyx orch start` calls it first, so one command still starts everything; never at machine start.
- The orch watcher and the beam daemon are two different programs.
  The daemon is named `dobby`, after the loom mechanism that lifts the shafts by pattern, since "beam" names the worktree.
  As a creel sender it is the program `DOBBY`: `ly:DOBBY` for the root beam and `ly:<slug>:DOBBY` for another beam.
- Beam and dobby are one module: `lyx beam` holds the commands (`create`, `promote`, `start`), and dobby is that module's daemon, as the watcher is orch's.

## Who does what (operator decisions, 2026-10-18)

- The orch is the LLM the operator talks to: it discusses, writes notes and tasks on the board, and takes the escalations that need judgement (parent review, PR-Gate when the alignment agent escalates, design questions).
  It never starts, stops or cleans up a batten run.
- Dobby sets everything going and cleans up: it starts tasks, follows their batten runs, revives dead drivers, settles mechanical stops by rule, lands and cleans up, and hands on what it cannot settle, first to the arbiter and then to the nearest orch.
  It writes the board only for statuses and the prune, and makes no design call.
- Batten drives one task's lifecycle as today and knows nothing of who owns its run.

## Draft tasks (operator decisions, 2026-10-18)

The operator often plans ahead by putting tasks on the board with their `depends_on` set, so a task is no longer by definition ready to be spawned.
A task carries a boolean field `draft` of its own, apart from `status`, which stays the run state.
`draft: true` means the task is not yet fully described; a new task is a draft by default.
Dobby starts a task only when it is not a draft and its `depends_on` are done; clearing `draft` on a task whose dependencies are done is how a task is started by hand.
The operator can clear the flag themselves, and dobby then starts the task with no orch involved.
A draft task keeps its dependencies visible in the README, in its Ready or Layer section with its After column, marked as a draft.

Orch recommendation, not a decision: the mark is a `Draft` column or a badge before the title, and the flag is cleared with a board verb such as `lyx board undraft <slug>`.

## Readiness without batten notices (operator decision, 2026-10-19)

Batten's landing notice no longer names newly ready tasks; dobby computes readiness itself from the board (kind task, not draft, `depends_on` done, not claimed).
The `newly ready` part of the notice, and the orch's start-on-notice step, go away when dobby lands.

Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-19): with dobby up, batten notices to the orch are hardly needed any more, and every kind of batten notice is to be revised in this light.

## Tender and dobby (2026-10-19)

Seen: `lyx tender` (pause, resume, revive, status) overlaps dobby's job in three places.
`tender revive` nudges sessions stalled on an API error, while dobby is to revive dead drivers; `tender resume` woke no Plan-Write strand that had a background fork (2026-10-19), which dobby, following status files, could notice; and batten starts runs today without reading tender's pause entries.

Orch recommendation, not a decision: keep them apart, tender as the brake and dobby as the engine.
Tender stays one hub-wide switch, used by the operator and by hibernate, across every beam.
Dobby reads tender's pause entries and starts, lands and revives nothing in a paused hub or pair; after a resume it checks that each interrupted run came back.
Revive moves into dobby as an automatic step, and `lyx tender revive` stays as a manual button.

## Folded in from `orch-split` (2026-10-11 to 10-13)

### Seen (operator, 2026-10-11)

The operator follows the orch from the phone through Remote Control, but so much comes in to the orch (batten notices, parent-review requests, escalations, PR-Gate reviews, landing routines) that the conversation is hard to follow.

### Idea (operator, 2026-10-11)

Split the hub orchestrator into two agents:

1. The run driver, the repo's upper driver: it reads the board, starts batten runs, and takes the escalated questions (parent reviews, review escalations, PR-Gate, landings).
   The operator can talk to it, but should not need to.
2. The conversational orch: the agent the operator talks to.
   It discusses problems with the operator and updates the board.

### Open

- How a question the run driver cannot settle reaches the operator: through the conversational orch, or as a notice of its own.
  The operator can keep both agents on Remote Control and gets a notification from the run driver when it needs input (operator, 2026-10-11).
- Who writes what on the board: the run driver only claims, sets statuses and prunes, while scope edits and notes stay with the conversational orch, or both write freely.
- How an operator decision reaches the run driver (start this bundle, change a hub config), and how the run driver learns the operator's settled decisions it needs at parent review.
- How much of the run driver is an LLM at all: most of the run loop is mechanical, as loom's driver now is; see `orch-owns-the-loop`.
  Starting a batten run on each ready board task (kind task, `depends_on` cleared, not claimed) needs no LLM (operator, 2026-10-11); nor does the landing routine.
  What the orch adds by hand today would need a home: per-task loom settings such as `review_max_bounces: 2` for a small task (a board field), and a cap on concurrent runs.
- `runs-overview` and `orch-token-spend` touch the same split.

### Idea: the run driver as a Go program (operator, 2026-10-12)

Perhaps the part split out of the orch is a Go-driven program: Go handles most of it on its own (starting ready tasks with their run settings, landings) and brings in the orch only when something goes wrong.
The same shape as loom today: the Go shed engine steps the run on its own (`lyx shed step --until-stop`), and the LLM driver above it wakes only when shed stops on something it cannot pass.
Per-task run settings (`config-layers-run-settings`) carry a task's review budgets and step models, so a start needs no LLM to set them.

### Two tiers, as in `go-driver-assistant` (2026-10-12)

`go-driver-assistant` (running) builds this shape for one loom run: a Go driver that settles stops by rule, a cold cheap assistant (the tackler) spawned only at a stop no rule settles, and the arbiter behind it.
The same two tiers fit the repo level:

1. A Go run driver: starts ready tasks with their `run_settings`, runs the landing routine (Land row, prod, intake), and posts what it cannot settle.
2. A spawnable assistant, cold per stop, never kept warm: it reads the stop and answers with a verdict or hands the question to the conversational orch.
   Scope and design choices always go to the orch.

Evidence from the loom level, a driver count over 98 runs (2026-10-05..12, 392 stops):

- plain relaunch 12 %; mechanical fix a Go rule could do 52 %; repair that needed an LLM 0 %;
- arbiter called 5 % (11 real attempts, all `resume`); relayed to the orch 22 %; other 10 %;
- drivers lived 370 h, 93 % of it idle.

The agent that ran the count estimated a cold helper would be needed at about 1 stop in 12 runs once Go takes the mechanical stops.
Nobody has counted the hub level yet: the orch's parent reviews, escalations, PR-Gates and landings by hand would need the same split before the Go share is known.

### A landing check for the Go run driver (operator, 2026-10-13)

At landing, loom warns that a task branch changed per-worktree config files (`_lyx/config/*.yaml`), which landing does not carry to the parent, and asks the parent to re-apply each change meant for it.
`logging-cleanup` raised it for a new, empty `_lyx/config/loom.yaml`: nothing to re-apply, and the orch found that only by diffing the file by hand.
The operator sees that check as a job for the Go run driver:

- parse the file at the fork base, the task tip and the parent tip, and compare keys;
- stay silent when the tip changes no key (an empty file, comments only) or the parent already holds the tip's value;
- otherwise name each changed key with its base, tip and parent values, so the parent knows exactly what to re-apply.


## Operator decisions (2026-10-24)

- The beam commands are `lyx beam create`, `lyx beam promote` and `lyx beam start`, as above.
- The workspace texts say beam, not umbrella; the task that builds a part renames the word in what it touches.
- The hub keeps lyx traces 3 days, not 14 (`logger.yaml` `trace_retention_days`, set on Bolt).
- Folded in from note `board-tidy-after-landing`: the beam's Go driver spawns the board-tidy Sonnet agent every N landings, N a config key defaulting to 5 (operator, 2026-10-24), in a window of the beam's reed session, and hands its report to the orch LLM (today the orch does it, hub-wide orch rule "Board tidy after a landing").

## The arbiter for every shed run (folded in from note `shed-arbiter-all`, 2026-10-24)

- Seen: loom and darn fill `sheddriver`'s optional `Arbiter` seam (`internal/loomcli/drivewiring.go`), so their stop chain is rule table, tackler, arbiter, orch; batten's own run fills only the tackler (`internal/battencli/drive.go`), so a stop the tackler escalates goes straight to the orch. `shed-tackler`'s decision record put this out of scope on purpose.
- Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15): the stop chain is the same for every shed run, and the arbiter is there to take load off the orch. The driver kind and the stop chain's settings are settable per repo, worktree layer included.
- Idea: move the arbiter into shed beside the tackler, its seam wired for every shed-driven recipe, batten and dobby included, its keys (`arbiter`, `arbiter_timeout_min`, `arbiter_max_spawns`, today in `loom.yaml`) in `shed.yaml` with per-module overrides; give the arbiter a description of batten's rows so it can judge a batten stop.

entries.title: Audit the twill and lens review setup: worth per perch, recurring finding classes, writer quality
entries.brief: One audit over the review records once about ten loom runs with the current setup land on Neve
entries.body:
## Questions

One audit over the same records (review files in the weft archive tags, `lyx report convergence`, `tools/tokencount/tokencount.sh`) answers three questions:

1. Is the lens fan and twill fixer setup worth its cost at each perch, and what should the standard review rounds be?
2. Which finding classes recur at Plan and Discussion, and where is each cheapest to stop at the source?
3. The open parts of the twill writer quality audit below, under "Data that would settle the open parts".

## When (operator, 2026-10-22)

Run it once about ten loom runs with the current setup have landed on Neve; runs from OSL-1046 are not gathered for it.

Later the same day (operator): run it now, over the loom runs landed since `504c5552` (2026-10-20), with the runs after `research-in-discussion` and `lenses-language-sets` (2026-10-22), which change Discussion, reported apart.

## Result of the first run (2026-10-22)

A sonnet agent ran the audit over the 6 loom runs landed since `504c5552`; the sample is small and only `finalize-dirty-names-paths` ran Discussion after the 2026-10-22 changes.

- Late rounds still pay: discussion round 3 found something real in 3 of 3 runs that reached it, plan round 2 in 3 of 3, nearly all new findings rather than too-narrow earlier fixes, so lowering caps is not supported.
- The lens fan raised 93% of round-1 gating findings at Discussion and 58% at Plan, for about $1 a perch; a review perch costs about $10-11, mostly in its later rounds.
- No further cut in round-1 findings from twill-plan is visible, and none is ruled out.
- Agent recommendation, not a decision: template defaults Discussion 2 soft / 3 hard, Plan 1 soft / 2 hard, Webster 1, Merge 1 (profile `light`'s values).
  Since `fed963ec5` these are no longer `light`'s values: the ladder is `speed`, `light` (1 round per perch), `solid` (Discussion 2, Plan 2) and `wide`.

## Operator decision (2026-10-22): lens fan in Discussion round 2

Since late rounds still find new things, Discussion-Review round 2 also runs the lens fan, and round 3 on runs solo: the hub's `loom.yaml` sets `discussion_reviewer_fan: ["review-discussion", "review-discussion", ""]`.
The twill fixer stays in every round, since many late-round defects are introduced by a sloppy fixer.
The next run of this audit checks what round 2's fan finds against a solo round 2, before Plan gets the same.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-22): fewer, sharper lenses

Tokens could be saved by scoping each lens more precisely and having fewer of them.
A later run of this audit, with more material, measures per lens what it finds that no other lens or the plain reviewer finds, and how much of it is real, so lenses can be merged, sharpened or dropped.
The Plan writer's `twill-plan` fan comes first: the Plan lead carries a large context, and each of its lens forks inherits it, while the Discussion lead's context stays small.

## Review rounds after twill-plan (was note `review-rounds-after-twill-plan`)

The earlier audit below found discussion-review round 3 and plan-review round 2 useful only when an earlier round's fix was too narrow.
Since `504c5552` (2026-10-20), the Plan writer's `twill-plan` fan runs every `review-plan` lens, as the Discussion writer's fan already runs every `review-discussion` lens, which should cut round-1 findings further.
Compare those runs' round-1 Plan findings against the earlier audit's baseline, and check whether discussion-review round 3 and plan-review round 2 still find anything; if they rarely do, lower the default review bounce caps for those segments.

## Review setup

### Seen (2026-10-18)

- On 2026-10-16/17 every perch got the reworked review setup: a lens fan in round 1 (`review-discussion`, `review-plan`, `review-code` beside a plain reviewer), a twill fixer every round, and twill writers for Discussion and Plan.
- The setup costs tokens and time at every perch, and no measurement yet shows what it catches that the plain setup missed.

### Operator decision (2026-10-18)

- Audit the use of the twill and lens setup across every perch once it has run for a while, and set the standard review rounds from the result (see `run-profiles`).

### Orch recommendation, not a decision

- Run it after about ten loom runs with the setup, from `lyx report convergence` (stop classes, fresh-code fixes, review rounds per segment), `tools/tokencount/tokencount.sh` and the review files in the records repository.
- Per perch: how many findings each fan member and round raised, how many led to a change that stayed, how many the later perches or PR-Gate would have caught anyway, and the tokens and minutes each round cost.
- Compare with the runs from before 2026-10-16 where the records allow it.

## Plan writer finding classes (was note `plan-writer-finding-classes`)

### Seen (2026-10-15)

Over the 15 most recent full loom runs (`tools/tokencount/tokencount.sh -last 15`), Plan cost about $13 a run: the plan lead about $5.50, its forks (fork0 and the five lens forks) about $4, and Plan-Burler-Review about $3.80.
Each fix the lenses or the review ask for is work the writer did not get right the first time.

### Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15)

Plan is heavy by nature, since it turns the Discussion into concrete work; the aim is a smarter Plan writer, so fewer Burler rounds are needed.

### Idea (orch recommendation)

- A fresh agent classifies every finding the Plan lenses and Plan-Burler-Review raised in recent runs: what kind of defect, whether it was real, and whether the review found something the lenses had not.
- Each recurring class goes where it is cheapest to stop at the source:
  - a machine check in `lyx loom validate-plan`, when the class can be checked deterministically;
  - a writer rule in the Plan stencil, when it is a judgement the writer can make up front;
  - a missing input, when the writer lacked something it needed (for example what `discussion-relevant-list` now hands it).
- Then measure whether lens and review findings per run drop.

### Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-16)

The lens fan and twill fixer (`fan-prompt-tuning`) are built first.
Later, this audit runs over real runs made with them, and the wording of the reviewer and fixer prompts is adjusted from what it observes, beside the Plan writer measures above.

### Operator decision (2026-10-16)

The Discussion and Plan perches run the twill fixer in every round; the lens fan reviewer runs in round 1 only, with solo review from round 2.
Reason: fixers introduce many defects, and a defect a late-round fixer introduces is seen only by the next review, or not at all at the hard cap.
The hub's `loom.yaml` carries it as `discussion_fan: ["review-discussion", ""]`, `plan_fan: ["review-plan", ""]`, `discussion_fix_fan: fix-discussion` and `plan_fix_fan: fix-plan`.
Orch recommendation, not a decision: the audit compares late-round fixer defects against runs from before this setup.

### Moved from note `perch-review-analysis` (issue #676, 2026-10-16)

The analysis measured rounds, tokens and late BLOCKING findings per perch; its classification of the late BLOCKING findings moved to `fan-prompt-tuning`, the lens fan and twill fixer it proposed are built there, and its proposal of two parallel round-1 reviewers is replaced by the lens fan.
Its Webster proposal (a hard cap of 2) is already met by the hub's `loom.yaml`: `webster_max_bounces: 1` with `webster_auto_accept: true`.
Two of its proposals are left for this audit to weigh, numbered as in the original:

3. **Later rounds review the fix delta.**
   A findings cannot be caught in round 1; they need a round after the fix.
   From round 2, one reviewer checks only what the fixer changed plus the sibling decisions or cards it touches, which is cheaper than a full review.
   Compare Traycer's incremental re-verify in #671.
6. **Measure again in a week**, with the same scripts: rounds per perch, BLOCKING share in round 1, and tokens per perch, before and after twill and the changes above.

## Twill writer quality, earlier result (was note `twill-writer-quality-audit`)

### Question (operator, 2026-10-18)

Has the quality of Discussion and Plan output gone up since the writers became twill-based?
An agent answered it on 2026-10-18 from the records (weft archive tags, Bolt config history, `lyx report convergence`); below is its finding.

### Short answer

Plan output got better when its writer became twill-based.
Discussion is the same or slightly better, which the data cannot show with confidence.
Adding the fork0 plan writer and the code list (generation 3) shows no further gain.

### Method

The main signal is round-1 BLOCKING plus MEDIUM findings of landed loom runs, read from the front matter of each run's `round-1-review.md` in the weft archive tags.
Each run is put in a generation by when its writer row started, checked against prod deploys and the hub config history on Bolt:

| Change | Live from | Set by |
|---|---|---|
| twill Discussion writer | 10-11 15:51 | `afd52a6f6` |
| twill Plan writer | 10-12 10:25 | `6099cd2bf` |
| fork0 plan writer (`2abb06c5e`) | 10-15 08:35 | deploy |
| code list (`530c339e9`) | 10-15 18:13 | deploy |
| review fan (`112cccb8f`) | 10-16 16:40 | `e57361ba5` |

Confounders and how they were handled:

- Baseline window 10-08 21:38 to 10-16 16:40, where every round-1 review ran solo on `opus[medium]` with no fan; earlier runs flipped reviewer between sonnet and opus (BLOCKING rate 0.69 against 1.32 per run) and are left out, as is `webster-replan-state`, which had a fan.
- After `112cccb8f` only five runs exist (`pr-gate-run-identity`, `creel-cli-output-fixes`, `shedrecipe-capabilities`, `creel-notices`, `orch-rules-files`); they are reported apart, not compared. The fan raises counts about 1.6x (5.4 to 8.8 findings per run at Discussion), matching 14 against 9.5 in `burler-fan-tuning-bench-2026-10-16`.
- `a273d69bc` only renamed keys; the models stayed the same (`25cc04048`).

### Signals

G1 is before twill, G2 twill, G3 fork0 plus code list.

Round-1 BLOCKING+MEDIUM per run (± standard error), and runs with any BLOCKING:

| Segment | G1 | G2 | G3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plan | 3.77±0.40, 26/40 runs | 1.72±0.30, 9/29 | 2.03±0.28, 12/33 |
| Discussion | 4.43±0.27, 20/28 | 3.57±0.27, 39/58 | 2.93±0.30, 6/15 |

- The first Plan runs (10-10 morning) are inflated by the switch to glyph-based plans (`78a2b1f14`); with Plan runs from 10-10 13:00 only, G1 is still 3.17.
- By task size in cards (diff size could not be resolved): the Plan drop holds in every bucket, 5.6 to 3.0 (over 12 cards), 2.9 to 1.7 (7 to 12), 2.2 to 0.4 (6 or fewer); G3 sits at or slightly above G2 (3.8, 2.5, 1.3). Discussion drops less: 5.3 to 4.8, 4.2 to 3.6, 3.8 to 2.3. G3 tasks are smaller (6.6 to 7.3 cards against about 10), and per card G3 Discussion is back at baseline (0.44 against 0.46).

Plan finding kinds per run, keyword counts over summaries, checked by reading about 15 runs:

| Plan finding kind, per run | G1 | G2 | G3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| design class | 1.43 | 0.62 | 0.48 |
| duplicate or over-specified tests | 0.38 | 0.03 | 0.15 |
| edits or tests no card targets | 0.35 | 0.14 | 0.12 |
| gate or glyph format | 0.75 | 0.31 | 0.12 |
| test branch no planned test reaches | 0.28 | 0.17 | 0.18 |

G1 runs such as `quick-recipe`, `config-layers-run-settings` and `driver-arbiter` are full of duplicate-test and missing-refusal-row findings, which the twill-plan lens forks target.
Discussion findings are the same kind in every generation, design holes such as unstated bounds and false premises (`lyx-halt`, `convergence-plan`, `fan-prompt-tuning`); design-class findings fall from 3.4 to 2.3 to 1.8 per run.
Wrong code references are rare in every generation and were not separated.

Rounds to converge, and circling settled by decision:

- Plan: 2.10 (5/40 circling), 1.69 (4/29), 1.61 (3/33).
- Discussion: 2.43 (10/28), 2.50 (21/58), 2.27 (2/15).
- Only `shuttle-send` (before 10-08) hit a hard cap.
- Rounds are confounded by Bouncer changes (`0ebdea27f` 10-08, `b2e4cf913` 10-11, `072e2ed86` 10-13, `85a8f3434` 10-14) and by sonnet reviewers in later rounds from 10-14 20:16 (Plan) and 10-15 07:30 (Discussion); within G2 circling halves after `072e2ed86` (14 to 7) with no writer change.

Plan gate failures: the Go gate retried Plan-Write once in the whole set (`tender`); the twill writers run `validate-plan` inside their session, so their failures are not in the records; no Plan-Write reran after 10-10 except `discussion-multi-llm`.

Downstream:

- Webster stops: G1 5/40 (`daemon-wakeups`, `test-suite-weight`, `driver-context`, `cli-surface`, `quick-recipe`), G2 2/29 (`tender`, `overview-seats` with plan_drifted), G3 0/33.
- Webster review rounds 1.98, 1.48, 1.12, but many Webster changes landed in the same window, so this is not credited to the writers.
- Webster deviations left out: their definition changed twice (`30385e1ae`, `493c62b71`).
- PR-Rework: G1 2/40 (`discussion-multi-llm`, `reed-hygiene`), G2 3/29 (`convergence-plan`, `reed-window-order`, `twill-fork0`), G3 1/33 (`creel-core`); no trend.
- Decisions added after Discussion: G1 11/28 runs (33 entries), G2 17/58 (37), G3 0/20; mostly parent design calls at circling escalations, which fell when `072e2ed86` and the alignment agent (`a40c7baef`) landed, so no writer signal.

### Verdicts

- Plan, G1 to G2: better, moderately high confidence. Round-1 BLOCKING+MEDIUM fell about 50% (about 3 standard errors even against the later G1 runs), in every size bucket, concentrated in the defect kinds the twill-plan lenses check; part of the format drop is glyph format settling.
- Plan, G2 to G3: same, low to moderate confidence. The bench predicted sharper fork0 lens catches (`twill-fork0-bench.md`); production shows no extra drop. The review rubric also changed in G3 (`9ea1f7474`, `e131c7625`, `27657341c`), and the code list (`530c339e9`) is mainly a cost change.
- Discussion: same or slightly better, low confidence. The 0.86-finding drop is about 2 standard errors, rounds did not move, the finding kinds did not change, and G3 is smaller tasks with the same findings per card; this matches `twill-discussion-bench.md` (contaminated, inconclusive) and `twill-discussion-fork0-bench.md` (keep twill, no fork0).

### Data that would settle the open parts

1. Blind real/noise grading of round-1 findings, as the bench grading did, on about 10 matched runs per generation.
2. A production replay: single writer against twill on 5 to 10 landed tasks from the solo-review window, with the same reviewer.
3. Plan-Write transcripts, to count `validate-plan` failures inside the session.
4. More runs under the fan review, for a post-`112cccb8f` baseline.
5. Diff sizes: for 113 of 179 runs the batch commits cannot be resolved in the prime, so only cards normalize size.

entries.title: Every remote operation runs async, and local-only fabric pairs stay an explicit choice only
entries.brief: Remote work goes async except the branch-exists check; batch pairs reach origin like any pair, and the local-only mode stays only as an explicit --local until a use is found or it is removed
entries.body:
## Seen

`batten-start-speed` builds local-only fabric pairs (`fabric add --local`, a local-only branch mark in `gitrepo` with a push refusal, pushes that skip such branches, and local modes of `fabric remove` and `fabric cleanup`): about 630 lines of code, 1360 with tests, plus a local-mark check in the status-push spawn entry.
The mode came from an orch recommendation in `weaver` that batch pairs never reach origin, which was wrong: a batch pair's commits are part of the implementation, and an agent continuing the work on another machine must see what a batch left half done.
The time it saves is small: in the sandbox hub `lyx fabric add` took about 1.1 s, nearly all of it two synchronous `git ls-remote` origin probes, with local work about 50 ms and its push already async; `lyx fabric remove --remote` took 6 to 7 s of network, at teardown, where nothing waits on it.

## Decisions (operator, 2026-10-18)

- The local-only pair mode stays for now, only as an explicit `fabric add --local` choice, since local work that needs no remote (experiments, local testing) may use it; no lyx flow creates local pairs, batch pairs included.
  Remove it (`--local`, the local-only branch mark and its push refusal, the skipped-local reporting in pushes, the local modes of remove and cleanup, and the local-mark check in the status push) if no use turns up.
- Every operation against a remote runs async, so no lyx command waits on the network.
  This includes `fabric remove`'s 6 to 7 s of network at teardown (force-with-lease push, archive-tag push, weft branch delete).
- One exception may stay synchronous: the check whether a pair's branches already exist on origin, since a branch found there is fetched and the work continued on, and that is worth waiting for.
  Today that is `fabric add`'s `git ls-remote` probes; they may run in parallel to cut the wait.

## Open

- Which remote operations are synchronous today besides `fabric remove`'s (force-with-lease push, archive-tag push, weft branch delete); an audit of the call sites belongs to the task that builds this.
- How an async remote failure reaches the operator or the orch.

entries.title: lyx batten run starts in its own window by default
entries.brief: Every batten run is started with --window, so the window should be the default and foreground the opt-in.
entries.body:
## Seen

The orch starts every run with `lyx batten run <slug> --window`, and the operator confirms that this is always how runs are started.
Without the flag the whole lifecycle runs in the caller's foreground for hours, which blocks the orch session and can be killed by the shell timeout.

## Idea

Make the window the default for `lyx batten run`: start the run in its own tmux window of the prime's reed session, return at once, and run the Open-Window row.
Keep the foreground as an explicit opt-in flag for the cases that need it, such as the window's own inner invocation and tests.
Update the orch role and the `lyx batten run` help to drop `--window` from the normal path.

## Done (2026-10-20)

The before and after measurement of `-trimpath` is in `docs/benchmarks/gate-test-xdr.md`.
The `go_parallel` sweep at 4, 8 and 12 is in the same file (`03af4c75`): no value gave a real gain, 8 was 6 % under 4 while two runs at 4 differed by 36 s, and no run failed, so `go_parallel` stays 4.

## Seen in the sweep

With `-trimpath` the build is reproducible: a fresh `GOCACHE` links byte-identical test binaries whose hashes XDR already knows, so it holds none of them.
The sweep forced new hashes with a random `-ldflags=-B` build ID, and even then few packages were held; `internal/fabricengine` (117-175 s) bounds the tier's wall time, and the rise at 8 and 12 is contention.

## Still open

The case the sweep set out to cover is unmeasured: a refill after a real change to a widely imported package, such as `internal/logger`, which showed about 50 held packages and a verify of about 6 min.
Whether a higher `-p` overlaps those holds needs one such run at 4 and one at 8.

entries.title: Discussion scope check moves from the alignment agent into the perch lenses, with an escalating finding class
entries.body:
## Seen

The alignment agent runs at two points of a loom run (`internal/alignment`): `parent-review`, after Discussion-Write's mechanical gate and before the Discussion perch, and `pr-gate`, after Publish.
At `parent-review` it checks the discussion against the board entry, the board, the in-flight runs' records (`lyx loom peers`) and the parent's landed commits, and approves, rejects or escalates to the orch.
The Discussion perch already covers most of that: lens `goal-scope` (in fans `discussion` and `twill-discussion`) checks the record against its board entry, and lens `board-fit` (in `twill-discussion`) checks it against every other board entry.
The name is stale too: the parent no longer reviews at that point, so neither the gate nor `lyx loom review` should say parent-review.

## Idea

Drop the alignment agent at the discussion point and keep it at `pr-gate`, where it approves the landing and names the board entries a run superseded:

- `board-fit` also reads the other in-flight runs' records through `lyx loom peers` and the parent's landed commits.
- A lens gets a finding class that escalates to the run's parent instead of going to the fixer, for a question only the operator can settle: a design conflict with another run, or doubt about what the task is for.
  The Bouncer routes such a finding up to the orch.
  Since `decision-reaches-agents` (2e265a4fc) the `decision` finding class exists and the Burler fix row posts it to the parent and keeps it from the fixer; what is left is the Bouncer's routing.
- The `parent-review` gate and the `lyx loom review` verbs go, and with them the parent-review name.

Gain: one cold agent spawn fewer per loom run.
Cost: the scope check no longer runs before the first perch round, so a round can be spent polishing a record whose scope then changes.

Discussed with the operator 2026-10-22; the operator agreed to record it as a note, the design is not yet decided.

entries.title: A plainly outdated task entry goes to the parent: from the Discussion review in loom, from Darn-Write in darn
entries.brief: No pre-Discussion row: board-fit flags an outdated entry as an escalating finding; Darn-Write checks and asks the parent
entries.body:
## Seen

A task's board entry is written when it is promoted, and can sit for days while other work lands and other runs start.
Its text reaches Discussion-Write and Darn-Write as it stands, so a scope that overlaps, contradicts or has been overtaken by other planned or landed work is found late, after a whole Discussion or a whole darn change has been written from it.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-24)

No new row runs before Discussion, and the board's run lock gets no exemption: an outdated entry is caught by work the run already does, and goes to the parent.

- Loom: the Discussion review's `board-fit` lens gets a finding class "the entry is plainly outdated" (overtaken by landed work, contradicted by the board or another run).
  Such a finding escalates to the parent orch instead of going to the fixer.
  This is the escalating finding class note `discussion-alignment-into-lenses` describes; the two belong together.
- Darn: it has no Discussion review, and Darn-Write reads the entry and writes code in one go.
  So Darn-Write itself checks the entry text against the parent's recent landed commits and the board before it starts, and when the text is plainly outdated it asks the parent and waits instead of guessing.

Only a plainly outdated entry goes to the parent; an ordinary small misalignment is settled by the writer as today.

## Replaces

An earlier idea (2026-10-22): a row before Discussion-Write and Darn-Write that aligns the entry text and edits its own entry through a run-lock exemption.
Dropped: it costs an LLM call in every run while most entries are fresh, and needs a lock exemption.

entries.title: Move rules about lyx behaviour out of this repo's CLAUDE.md into lyx code, doc.go and stencils
entries.body:
## Seen

This repo's `CLAUDE.md` holds rules about how lyx itself behaves, which hold for every repo developed with lyx, not only this one.
Examples: in "Docs land in the same commit", that the task that builds a design never changes its own board entry's body or scope, that the landing marks the entry done and the board prune removes it, and that no decision, card or step of a run changes the running task's own entry; in "Production", how Batten's Land row runs the hub's `deploy` command and how `alignment_pr_approve` withdraws the alignment agent's landing.

## Idea

Two kinds of rule must be kept apart (operator, 2026-10-22):

1. Rules for every use of lyx, in any repo: they apply locally, to the repo the hub develops.
   They ship with lyx: what lyx enforces lives in the code and its package `doc.go`, and what agents must be told lives in the stencils lyx ships, so every hub gets them.
2. Rules for developing LoomYard itself, here in this repo: they live in this repo's `CLAUDE.md`, such as the cgo build, `update-plugins.sh` and the push rule for `main`.

Mixing them breaks other hubs: when the quarry hub was set up as a LYXHUB repo, its orch began taking in the LoomYard repo's issues instead of quarry's own, because a rule written for LoomYard development was read as a lyx rule.
`CLAUDE.md` is for one repo only, so go through it and move every rule of kind 1 out into lyx; go through the stencils too for rules of kind 2 that name LoomYard where they should name the hub's own repo.

The run-lock rule in `CLAUDE.md` (no decision, card or step of a run changes the running task's own entry) is a rule of kind 1: its home is the board's run lock and its package `doc.go`, so it moves out with the rest.

entries.title: Lens overlap audit: which lenses find the same defects, and a smaller set
entries.brief: twill-plan 8 to 5 lenses recommended; twill-discussion 7 to 4 and review-code 4 to 3 at low confidence
entries.body:
## Question (operator, 2026-10-22)

Which lenses find the same defects, which defect areas the lenses essentially cover, and whether a smaller lens set covers the same ground.

## Result (sonnet agent, 2026-10-22)

Sources: `_lyx/plan/lens-review.md` in the weft archive tags (94 loom runs, only 6 of them, all on 2026-10-22, with all 8 `twill-plan` lenses), the per-lens fork reports in the machine-local Claude Code transcripts (5 runs), and per-lens attribution in `round-1-review.md`.
The sample with the full lens set is small, lens texts changed over time, and a "fixed" finding only means the writer agreed; since `lens-fork-reports-kept` landed (79bab47a0) every lens fork's report is kept verbatim beside its record (`*.lens-<lens>.md` under `_lyx/plan/`, `_lyx/discussion/` and the review rounds), so later audits have per-lens data.

### `twill-plan` (8 lenses)

- `affected-set` and `forced-edits` are near-duplicates: 12 of `affected-set`'s 20 findings were also raised by `forced-edits`, 5 were its alone.
- `criteria-coverage`, `branch-coverage` and `row-reachability` overlap heavily; in one run all three reports led with the same three defects.
- `guard-reach` and `way-forward` overlap little with anything and each raised BLOCKING findings no other lens did.
- `test-economy` is 79% LOW and the most disputed, but its findings are unique.

Agent recommendation, not a decision: 5 lenses.

| Proposed lens | Replaces |
| --- | --- |
| `coverage` | `criteria-coverage`, `branch-coverage` |
| `row-validity` | `row-reachability`, `test-economy`, the nil-seam part of `affected-set` |
| `forced-edits` | `affected-set`, `forced-edits` |
| `guard-reach` | unchanged |
| `way-forward` | unchanged |

Merging `guard-reach` and `way-forward` as well is not supported by the data.

### `twill-discussion` (7 lenses), low confidence

No lens-review file exists for the Discussion writer; one run's fork reports were read in full.
Agent recommendation, not a decision: 4 lenses, `decision-chain` (`interactions` + `walkthrough`, keeping the case-based procedure), `code-claims` (`bound-breaker` + `existing-paths`), `board-scope` (`goal-scope` + `board-fit`), `leanness`.
In the review fan, `bound-breaker` is the strongest lens (11 of 15 lens BLOCKING findings), `walkthrough` raised no BLOCKING.

### Review fans

- `review-plan` reruns the three lenses the Plan writer already ran, and still raised 35 findings in the six 2026-10-22 runs, mostly LOW and MEDIUM; whether these are bad fixes or new findings is not measured. Option: give `review-plan` the lenses the writer fan lacks.
- `review-code`: `code-affected-set` is the weakest (one MEDIUM in 18); agent recommendation, medium-low confidence: fold it into `code-pattern-fit`, which carries 7 of 8 lens BLOCKING findings, as one `code-consistency` lens, 4 to 3.
- `fix-*` fans: no per-lens data.

## Follow-up (operator, 2026-10-22)

- `twill-plan` goes to 5 lenses in task `twill-plan-five-lenses`.
- A later audit looks at the Discussion writer's `twill-discussion` alone, once enough runs made after 79bab47a0 have kept per-lens reports, and may trim it too.
  It matters less than Plan: the Discussion lead's context is far smaller when it forks, so its lens forks cost far less.

entries.title: Trial: batcher profile wide (budget 300k)
entries.brief: Hub runs a new batcher profile wide, budget 300k; check cost and fork quality before taking it into the template
entries.body:
## Seen

`run-process-ownership` (2026-10-22) ran mostly one card per fork under the `cautious` profile's budget 200k: its cards estimated 145-260k alone.
Measured fork peaks matched the estimates overall; `batch_growth` (7k) is above the ~2k measured when batches go well.
Many small forks were expensive under the identity batcher.

## Decision (operator, 2026-10-22)

`cautious` stays as it is; the hub's `batcher.yaml` adds a profile `wide`, the same as `cautious` but with `budget: 300000`, and makes it `active`.

## Follow-up

After a few loom runs, compare cost and fork quality against earlier runs; then decide whether `wide` goes into `internal/batcher/template.yaml`.

## First check (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-24)

The hub switched at 2026-10-22T15:50 (records commit `216c22a12`); each run's profile comes from its `_lyx/webster/state.json`.
Only 2 wide runs with a Webster record have landed (`orch-strand-cycle`, `loom-tail-review`, the latter run on another machine, so no cost data), against 51 cautious runs since 2026-10-15.

| median | cautious (51) | cautious, 10+ cards (18) | wide (2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| cards per fork | 3.0 | 2.1 | 3.1 |
| measured fork peak | 171k | 192k | 310k (1 run) |
| Webster cost per card | $1.15 | $1.50 | $1.12 (1 run) |
| review findings | 1 | 2 | 2 |

- Too few wide runs to decide; no quality regression seen (no stuck batches, one review round).
- In the one measured run, forks of 4-5 cards peaked at 310k and 315k, 31-39% over the batcher's estimate; cautious forks average 0.99 of estimate. If `wide` stays, the estimator needs calibrating above 200k.
- Recheck after 6-8 more wide runs. Rerun with `docs/research/batch-budget-trial-2026-10-24/compare.sh [FROM-date]`; its README and the 2026-10-24 baseline tables sit beside it.

entries.title: Plan writer cost: sub-planners per part, and twill versus a solo writer
entries.brief: The Plan writer is 18% of spend; sub-planners per part for large bundles, and a twill versus solo Opus high comparison on cost, rounds and time
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: the Plan writer is the costliest session type, about $8 per run, $1,306 with its forks over two weeks (18% of all spend).
It averages 81 turns at a mean context of 223k, holds 153k by its first fork and peaks around 308k, mostly from about 71 raw `sed -n`/`grep` code reads.
Every `twill-plan` lens fork inherits that context, about 287k per turn; since 2026-10-20 the writer and its forks cost about $18 per run.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

Fork the lenses earlier, before the code reads pile up, or hand the writer a digest of the code it needs instead of raw reads.
Cutting a quarter of the writer's and its forks' cost saves about 4.5% of all spend; quality must be benched first.

## Discussion with the operator (2026-10-22)

- A code digest instead of raw reads is rejected: it is too inexact unless the code itself is read, and the writer would read the source anyway to be sure.
  Finding what to read is already `relevant.md`'s job; whether the writer uses it is worth measuring (how much of what the writer read the list named).
- Lens forks as fresh agents are rejected: that is the perch itself.
- Sub-planners: Discussion splits the scope into parts in the decision record, groups `relevant.md` per part, and each sub-planner reads only its part; the lead owns the shared spots and joins the card DAG.
  This keeps every review round and matters more as loom tasks are bundled larger.
  Review could split per part the same way, since each fresh reviewer rebuilds its context every round (Plan reviewer: 48 turns at 123k mean context, $2.48 per session).
- Twill-plan versus a solo writer: since the full `twill-plan` fan (2026-10-20), 7 landed loom runs average 2.00 Plan rounds against 2.09 before, while the writer's forks cost about $7 per run and a Plan round about $3.70; too few runs to judge.
  The operator sees strong signs that the twill writer makes a far better one-shot plan in shorter time, and time counts as well as tokens.
  Still, test a solo Opus high writer: compare twill, solo Opus high and solo Fable on Plan cost, Plan rounds and Plan wall time (`lyx report timing`) per run.

## Split writing: two variants to bench (operator, 2026-10-22)

Discussion-Write and Plan-Write already run as `shedadapters.MultiLLMProducer` over a `seatengine` table, a chair and advisors; advisors only advise, and twill is the chair forking itself, so today one session writes the whole product.
Two ways to have parts written separately, both benched against each other and against the twill and solo writers before anything reaches production:

1. **Seats with writing assistants.** The chair splits the scope, fixes the interfaces and shared spots, and hands each assistant seat its part; it then joins and checks the parts.
   A new seat role beside the advisor.
   Risks: assistants see neither each other's work nor a shared context, so seams fall to the chair and review, and overlapping parts make several seats read the same code.
2. **Fork-based.** The chair keeps its context lean (scope, split and shared spots only) and forks once per part, so every part writer inherits the same overview without the writer's full reading.
   Technically still one writer with forks, like twill but forking early.

## Data check (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-24)

Plan writer plus its lens forks, means per run (API list price):

| group | runs | writer+forks | forks | Plan-Write wall | Plan rounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before 10-15 (solo writer) | 28 | $9.08 | $0.58 | 16.4 min active | 1.3 |
| 10-15 to 10-19 | 41 | $9.39 | $3.86 | 18.5 min | 1.88 |
| 10-20 to c62274be5 (full twill-plan fan) | 7 | $18.14 | $7.66 | 23.9 min | 2.00 |
| after c62274be5 (five lenses) | 3 | $16.64 | $7.40 | 23.9 min | 1.33 |

- The later groups are larger tasks, so the cost rise is not the fan alone; the five-lens group is too small to judge.
- `relevant.md` use, over 32 runs with a list and a Plan-Write transcript: 85% of named files were read, but only 28% of read files were named (about 3.5 files read per file named, about 7 on large runs). Both shares are lower bounds (directory greps and quarry reads not counted).
- So `relevant.md` works as a floor, not a boundary; most unnamed reading looks like tests and neighbouring callers, which a per-part split of the list would not remove.
- Still open: the solo Opus high and Fable writer bench, and the split-writing variants, which need new runs.
- Scripts, baseline tables and `results.md` are in `docs/research/plan-writer-audit-2026-10-24/`; rerun per its README.
