entries.title: Large tasks: Discussion, a pre-planner, and the pieces as darn runs inside the task's beam
entries.brief: Discussion decides scope, a pre-planner splits it into contracted pieces, each piece runs as darn from the task's beam, a whole-task perch reviews, then align and land
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-22)

A large task runs as a loom whose implementation is a set of darn runs inside its own beam:

1. Task A runs Discussion as today; Discussion stays the one agent that talks with the operator and decides scope.
2. A pre-planner breaks the decided scope into smaller pieces that together make up the whole scope.
   Each piece gets a contract: what it takes in, the behaviour it delivers, the names it exports to other pieces, and which pieces it depends on; not the inside, which the darn finds itself.
3. Each piece becomes a darn task with that contract and its part of the decision record and `relevant.md`, with `depends_on` between pieces.
4. The next producer turns Task A's worktree into a beam.
5. The darn tasks run from beam A as ordinary darn runs and merge back into Task A's branch, not `main`; pieces with no dependency between them run in parallel.
6. When every darn has merged back, a Task A-wide perch reviews the whole and makes small fixes.
7. The rest is as today: alignment, PR, landing, so `main` takes Task A whole.

## Why

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: a loom run carries a fixed cost of about $23, mostly Plan and the review rounds, and the Plan writer reads about 250k of context before it writes (91% of its peak).
Darn's fixed cost is about $2.60.
Split this way, each darn reads only its piece once, plans and implements it, and is reviewed by its own perch; Discussion and the whole-task perch keep loom's scope and overall check.
It came out of discussing sub-planners for the Plan writer (note `plan-writer-context`): pieces small enough to plan and implement together are darn runs.

## Depends on

The beam setup on the board: `orch-any-worktree` (umbrella tasks spawning and landing from their own worktree) and `umbrella-daemon` (a daemon per beam that drives its runs).

## Open

- Contract precision: too loose and pieces collide, too tight and the pre-planner becomes today's Plan writer.
- A darn that finds its contract wrong stops and escalates to Task A instead of improvising; dependent pieces wait.
- What drives the darns inside the beam: the beam's daemon or orch thread, and how Task A's run waits for them.
- How large the whole-task perch's fixes may be before they mean a piece failed.
- Quality against full loom: each piece gets one perch instead of Plan and Webster review; measure follow-up fixes against loom runs.
- Cost: Discussion, pre-planner, N darns and the whole-task perch against a loom run of the same size.

## Review placement (operator, 2026-10-22)

- The pre-plan gets a perch, but the pre-plan is far smaller than today's plan format: pieces and their contracts, not cards.
- No perch per darn: a review per batch proved far too expensive in Millhouse, and a perch per piece is the same.
  The pieces run as darn with review off (`code_max_bounces: 0`, since `code-review-one-perch` made darn's perch the Code-Review perch), each still passing its own gate and tests; the whole-task perch after the last merge-back is the code review, as Webster's round over the whole diff is today.
  For scale, a darn perch costs about $1.30 per run in the audit window.
- The pieces run tests as they go, the way Webster's card gate runs after every card.

## Piece recipe `stitch` (operator, 2026-10-22)

The pieces run on their own recipe, `stitch`, derived from darn, not on a darn profile: rows go away, not only bounds.
Alignment per piece is pointless when the piece is a closed, synchronised share of an umbrella that is aligned whole.

- Kept: Preflight; the writer, on Sonnet, briefed by its pre-plan contract.
- Dropped: Code-Bouncer and the Code-Burler review/fix rows (review off), Describe and PR-Review.
  Since `loom-tail-review` (2026-10-24) darn has no Merge-In, Publish, PR-Align or PR-Gate rows; its Finalize merges the parent in under the lock.
- Finalize merges into the umbrella branch under the parent lock instead of landing on `main`.
- Friction-Reflect runs once per umbrella, not per piece.
- A `stitch` task runs only inside an umbrella; it cannot run alone.
- Estimate (orch, not measured): about $2-2.50 per piece against about $6 for a darn with review.

Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-24): once `stitch` exists, Codex could run the pre-planner, as a role apart from the Claude-written code (see note `codex-engine`).

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-23): darn itself as the piece implementer

Once `loom-tail-review` has landed, darn itself may serve as the pieces' implementer, since that task removes much of the run tail's ceremony, such as the pull request.
Whether `stitch` then stays a recipe of its own, or becomes darn with the tail rows a piece does not need turned off, is to be weighed against what `loom-tail-review` lands.

## Test depth of a piece (operator, 2026-10-23)

A piece run does not run the full suite a standalone darn runs before it lands.
The umbrella runs the full suite once, after every piece has merged back.
Which tiers a piece's own gates run is open; the gate key per recipe row is stated in `internal/gateslot`'s doc (`gate-runs-once`, landed): a piece's rows read `darn-write`, `code-burler-fix` and `finalize`.

## Pre-plan depth (orch, 2026-10-24, not decided)

- A coarse pre-plan leaves design to the pieces, so each piece needs an Opus writer.
- A detailed pre-plan carries the design, so Sonnet pieces may do, at the cost of a heavier pre-planner.
- Pieces cannot be counted on to run in parallel: `tools/plandag/plandag.sh` on `loom-tail-review`'s plan found 52 cards, a critical path of 20 and a mean parallelism of 2.6.
  A beam's gain is then mostly smaller review scopes, not wall time.

entries.title: Ubuntu 24.04 as a stated and checked floor: a PATTERN entry and a mechanical check
entries.brief: A Neve-written reed change broke on tmux 3.4; nothing states or checks the Ubuntu 24.04 floor
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-10-23)

`e634efb9` separated the reed pane tail with `"\x1f"`, written and tested on Neve (Ubuntu 26.04, a newer tmux).
On OSL-1046 (Ubuntu 24.04, tmux 3.4), tmux prints the separator as the literal text `\037`, so the reed naming tests and a dead-strand test failed in every run cut before `a1200c20` switched to a tab.
Earlier tasks already made LoomYard run on Ubuntu 24.04.
Nothing states Ubuntu 24.04 as a supported floor: PATTERN names no platform floor, and the repository has no CI.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-23)

Everything must work on Ubuntu 24.04; checking that by hand all the time is a large job.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

- A PATTERN entry naming the floor: Ubuntu 24.04 with its tmux 3.4, its git and its Go toolchain, so a writer and a reviewer know what an external tool's behaviour may be assumed from.
- A mechanical check, so no one checks by hand, either:
  - a CI job on GitHub's `ubuntu-24.04` runner, tmux from apt, that runs the tiers up to the tmux tier on every push to `main`; or
  - the gate's tmux tier runs against a tmux 3.4 binary on every machine, so a run on Neve meets the floor's tmux too.
- OSL-1046 runs the tmux tier in every end gate since 2026-10-23 (then keyed `final` and `landing`, now `webster`, `merge-in` and `finalize`), so a run there already meets the floor; the gap is runs on Neve.


## From issue #848

Imported from [issue #848](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/848).

## What happened

Twice in one task run, the Publish row halted `blocked` (anomaly `escalation-to-human`) with "publish gate failed after merging parent branch main (exit code 1)".
Both gate runs (`lyx gate test` tier2) reported the same 8 failures, in two packages: `internal/reedcli` and `internal/reedengine`.

- `TestNaming/TaskWorktreeStrandNameTitleAndEnv`, `TestNaming/EmptySlugGivesShortnameAndRole`, `TestNaming/RepairNamesRestoresAHandChangedTitle` and their parent `TestNaming` (`internal/reedcli/naming_integration_test.go`): the pane title read back is the strand name followed by literal `\037` escapes and the shell name and path (shape `tc:helper\037bash\037/usr/bin/bash`), where the test wants `tc:helper`.
- `TestStrandNamingAndList/HubWideDirectoryAndDrift`: the same family, failing in the same package.
- `TestOwnWindow_RealTmux/ShellOnlyStrandReadsDeadPastTheGraceAndResumeRelaunchesIt` (`internal/reedengine/ownwindow_integration_test.go`): `Status` of a shell-only strand past the grace returns `Live:true`, where the test wants present and not live.

The failures were identical on the two runs, which differ only in what the Darn-Write pass changed in between.
The task itself changes the board engine, not reed.
The failures sit in code the task did not touch, so they are most likely environmental (the host tmux version's format output) or came in with the merged parent branch.

## Why it is abnormal

The recovery path the halt prescribes (`lyx loom goto --to Darn-Write`, then `lyx loom resume`) cannot fix a failure outside the task's files.
The loop was walked once and re-blocked at Publish with the same 8 failures, so the run needs the operator for a failure that no task change can clear.
The real-tmux tests also look host-sensitive: pane titles that include the `\037` separator suggest reed's title format string is not interpreted as a control character by this tmux, and a shell-only pane is judged alive past the grace.

## What to do

- Determine whether these real-tmux reed tests fail on the parent branch itself on this host, and if so fix them at the root: stop depending on a tmux format escape that this tmux version emits literally, and re-check the shell-only liveness rule.
- Consider having the Publish gate tell a failure the task introduced from one the merged parent already carries, so the halt note names it and does not send the run back to Darn-Write.

Provenance: task slug `prime-owner-visible`; notes `loom-halt.md`, `loom-halt-2.md`.

entries.title: Carry agent mail into the pane in full instead of a reminder and a read turn
entries.brief: A reminder plus lyx creel read costs the receiver an extra turn per agent message
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-23)

Creel carries a message in full into the receiver's pane only when its sender is a program or EXTERNAL.
Mail from an agent strand, and any message over 4 KiB, reaches the receiver only as a reminder line naming `lyx creel read` (`internal/creelengine/doc.go`), so the receiver spends one extra turn reading it before it can act.
The reminder exists so that an agent's text cannot pose as an instruction in another agent's pane.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-23)

With the runs' cost in focus, everything might instead be typed into the pane directly, with no reminder and read turn; to weigh later.

## To weigh

- The extra turn per agent message against the guard that keeps one agent's text from reading as an instruction in another agent's pane.
- Note `creel-agents` moves agent messaging from SendMessage onto creel, which makes agent mail, and so this cost, more common.

entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-24)

The prime moved from OSL-1046 back to Neve with `lyx adopt --prime`; nothing checked that the landed code builds and passes on the adopting machine.
Machines differ: Neve runs Ubuntu 26.04, OSL-1046 Ubuntu 24.04, OSL-1033 Windows 11, so code landed on one can break on another.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-24)

An adopt runs the test suite on the adopting machine, so a break the machine change brings shows at once, not inside the next run's gate.
Note `ubuntu-2404-floor` covers the stated floor and its mechanical check.

## Open

- Which tiers: the tiers of the `finalize` gate key (`lyx config gate`, `gates.finalize`), or tier 0 and 1 only.
  A tier already green for the clean tree is carried and runs nothing.
- Whether a red suite refuses the adopt, or only reports.
- Whether it runs in the background, so the adopt returns at once.

entries.title: Umbrella groundwork: project entries, pairs from a parent pair, and umbrella tasks that spawn and land from their own worktree
entries.brief: [WS 004+006] Board projects, fabric pairs from a parent pair, batten and orch from any worktree, umbrella tasks
entries.body:
## Bundle (operator, 2026-10-24)

One loom for the umbrella groundwork: `pair-from-parent` is the groundwork `orch-any-worktree` builds on, over the same packages.
Both notes date from 2026-10-18/19; check each part against the code as it stands, since adopt, owner machines, the prime owner and the new run tail have landed since.

# Part 1: groundwork (from `pair-from-parent`)

## Seen (2026-10-18)

- Fabric's `Add` forks a pair from the HEAD of the worktree it runs in (`internal/fabricengine/add.go`), and batten's Worktree-Create calls it from the prime (`internal/battencli/wire.go`), so every batten run forks from the prime's checked-out branch.
- Every batten verb refuses outside the prime (`RefuseUnlessPrime` in `internal/battencli`).
- After creation the parent is already per run: the origin record carries `ParentBranch` and `ParentWorktree`, loom and darn take `params.parent` from it, parent locks are per parent branch, and the Land row skips the prime pull and deploy when the parent is not the prime's branch (`internal/battenshed/land.go`).
- The board has no field grouping tasks or naming where a task's pair comes from.

## Operator decisions (2026-10-18, recorded in `orch-any-worktree`)

- A task carries one `project` field naming a project entry on the board.
- A project always groups its tasks, and the project entry says whether it has a worktree of its own; with one it is an umbrella, without one its tasks go to the prime.
- The project entry may hold the ordered list of its tasks, so the README shows it as a plan; the `workspaces` work is the first project, with no worktree of its own.
- An umbrella's branch is derived from its slug and fabric's `branch_prefix`; no branch name is hard-coded or stored.
- A task of an umbrella has its pair created from the umbrella's branch and lands there.

## Idea

The groundwork umbrellas need, built first:

- Board: project entries (with their own-worktree flag and ordered task list), the `project` field on tasks, and README grouping by project; useful at once for grouping-only projects such as `workspaces`.
- Fabric creates a pair from a named parent pair's branch rather than from the worktree it runs in.
- Batten's Worktree-Create creates the pair from the task's project when that project has a worktree, and batten verbs run from any worktree of the hub, keeping their shared state under the prime.
- Merge-back into the parent and teardown work unchanged, as they already follow the origin record.

`weaver`'s per-batch pairs need the same create-from-parent-pair, merge-back and teardown primitive.

## Folded in: board slug check and blocked-run cleanup (issue #724, operator decision 2026-10-18)

- Seen 2026-10-18: task `orch-rules-in-weft` was promoted and started, and batten blocked at Worktree-Create with an invalid slug, since a slug ending in `-weft` is reserved for weft worktrees.
  The orch cleared the run claim with `lyx board set-status`, renamed the entry to `orch-rules-files` with `lyx board merge` and started a new run; the old blocked batten record `_lyx/shed/orch-rules-in-weft` stays, since `lyx batten cleanup` skips blocked runs.
- Expected: `lyx board upsert` and `promote` refuse a task slug fabric cannot use, naming the rule, from one slug rule fabric owns; and a blocked run whose board entry is gone can be cleaned up.

# Part 2: umbrella tasks (from `orch-any-worktree`)

## Why

The operator works long-term on a branch of their own in its own worktree, not on `main`, which in a large project is not theirs to drive; that worktree is where they want their orch.
Today every `lyx orch` verb refuses outside the hub's prime (`internal/orchcli/refusal.go`), every batten verb does too (`RefuseUnlessPrime` in `internal/battencli`), and orch keeps its files under the prime's `.lyx/orch/`.
Run parentage already follows the worktree a pair was created from (`aa67fd1d7`, #341), so a pair created from the operator's worktree would land there; orch and batten are what stand in the way.

## Want

- `lyx orch` and `lyx batten` run from any drivable worktree in the hub, which then acts as that orch's home: pairs branch from its branch and land into it, and orch's scratch, handoffs and reed strand live in that worktree.
- More than one orch per hub, one per home worktree, without stepping on each other's pairs, board claims or reed sessions.

## Open points

- What "prime only" protects today and whether any of it must stay prime-bound (board writes, deploy, `lyx board prune`, the hub workspace).
- What the relevant CONSTRAINTS.md invariants say about prime (batten's prime-anchored status and lock paths, Told-Geometry) and how they change.
- Who starts a task that becomes ready: presumably its umbrella's thread, found through the task's `project`.

## Operator decisions (2026-10-18)

- A task carries one `project` field naming a project entry on the board (decision later the same day, replacing an earlier `parent` field).
  A project always groups its tasks; the project entry itself says whether it has a worktree of its own.
  A project with its own worktree is an umbrella; one without is a grouping only, and its tasks spawn from and land into the prime.
  The project entry may hold the ordered list of its tasks, so the README shows it as a plan and titles need no order prefix; the `workspaces` work is the first project, with no worktree of its own.
- An umbrella is a long-lived fabric pair that is a starting point with its own orch thread.
  It is not a separate hub: it shares the hub's repo, weft, board, creel daemon and gate slots, and has its own `.lyx/`, thread and batten runs.
- The prime is the root umbrella; a task with no `project`, or whose project has no worktree, goes to the prime.
  The umbrella's branch is derived from the slug and fabric's `branch_prefix` (so a work hub with `branch_prefix: hanf/` needs no thought about prefixes); no branch name is hard-coded or stored.
- A task's pair is created from its umbrella's branch and lands there, and the task's notices and escalations go to the umbrella's thread.
- The board is shared by the whole hub; an umbrella's thread sees and starts only its own tasks.
- An existing, spawned task can be turned into an umbrella: its pair and the commits on its branch stay, its loom run stops, a thread starts in the pair, and later tasks name it as their `project`.
  Giving a grouping-only project a worktree later is the same step, and its tasks need no change, since they name the project rather than a worktree.
  Since a run-held entry takes no board edits, this is a verb of its own that releases the run's lock.

## Operator decision (2026-10-18, later): beam and orch apart

An umbrella is now called a beam: a worktree plus a Go daemon, in the module `lyx beam` (see `umbrella-daemon`).
An orch thread is separate and optional: a beam runs its tasks with no orch, and what its daemon cannot settle escalates through the arbiter to the nearest orch up the beam chain, the prime last.

## Naming a beam's orch thread (2026-10-19, not decided)

The thread has no name of its own yet.
Operator view, not a decision: it can well be called orchestrator, since that is what it is.
Candidates:

- orchestrator (orch recommendation): run through `lyx orch` in every beam; its strand is `ly:orch` in the root beam and `ly:<slug>:orch` in another beam, matching dobby's `ly:DOBBY` and `ly:<slug>:DOBBY`.
- foreman: the lead on a building site; fits the workshop theme, but is one more word to learn.
- steward: the one who looks after a beam.

Weaver is ruled out (operator): it names the planned cold-start implementer beside Webster (note `weaver`).

## Operator views, not decisions (2026-10-18)

- At work the operator sets a branch of their own as their base and spawns large sub-projects from it, while smaller tasks still spawn from `main`.
- What the operator wants is a thread they can open in any worktree and hold a running conversation with, which can spawn everything from there.
  With two large projects at once, two such threads, one per project, which the operator talks to separately and which can talk to each other; they need not be called orchestrators.
- Millhouse supports this today: a thread anywhere creates a task and spawns it from its own worktree, the task records that thread and worktree as its parent, and it merges back there when done.
- The orch role should not be unique: any thread that starts another thread becomes its parent.
- Giving a thread the orch hosting (its own watcher and context cycling) is an explicit command; the hub orch is long-lived enough to need it, while a project thread is time-limited, so cycling matters less there but would be nice.
- Reed shows every session at once, which gets messy; the threads a project's thread starts should be grouped under it as one project.
- Nothing hub-wide is left for a thread: deploy and prune are in the Land row, and intake from GitHub issues runs on command.
- A thread that is not running is a real problem whatever the design, as it is for the orch today.
- Two hubs with two weft repos would work today, but would make exchanging information between them hard.

## Seen (2026-10-18)

- Batten's Worktree-Create calls fabric's `Add` from the prime (`internal/battencli/wire.go`), and `Add` forks from the HEAD of the worktree it runs from, so every batten run forks from the prime's checked-out branch.
- The parent is already per run after that: the pair's origin record carries `ParentBranch` and `ParentWorktree`, loom and darn take `params.parent` from it, parent locks are per parent branch, and the Land row skips the prime pull and deploy when the parent is not the prime's branch (`internal/battenshed/land.go`).
- The board has no field naming a task's parent today.
- Every file orch writes goes through one accessor, `internal/orchcli/paths.go`, under the prime's `<anchor>/.lyx/orch/`; `lyx orch` refuses outside the prime and its strand name carries no worktree (`agentname.RoleOrch`).

## Operator decision (2026-10-18): no process while an umbrella lives

An umbrella is not a shed run that waits for weeks, since nothing restarts a waiting process after a machine restart (today `lyx batten run <slug>` resumes from disk, but someone must run it).
It has work only at its start and its end:

1. Create: its pair, thread and workspace, in one short command.
2. Live: no process; it is a pair, a board task and a thread the operator talks to when they want.
3. Land: when the operator says the project is done, a short run does Merge-In, Publish, PR-Gate and Finalize into its own parent; that run may be a shed run, living only as long as the landing.

## Operator decision (2026-10-19): a beam has an owner machine

Task `machine-handover` gives every board entry an `owner` machine and a takeover verb; beams extend it:
- every task and every beam has its own owner machine, and each machine's dobby drives only the runs that machine owns;
- adopting a beam takes the beam only: its children keep their owners (this replaces an earlier same-day decision that the children go with it);
- a task lands into its parent by merging in the parent's local worktree, so a branch lands into a beam only on the machine that owns the beam;
- normally the parent's owner lands a finished run of another machine from its branch on origin, after a ready-to-land handover through Bolt (creel reaches only one machine), with no takeover;
- when that machine is not available, the landing machine adopts the parent first, without the old owner's help, and the old owner pauses what it no longer owns when it next wakes or starts its orch;
- landing a beam into its parent beam follows the same rule;
- `lyx adopt --all` takes over the whole hub;
- the origin check of `machine-handover` (`git ls-remote` over the warp and records repos) covers beam branches with no extra work.

## Orch sketch, not a decision

- A thread starts its runs itself with `lyx batten run`, which finds the prime for the shared state; the run records the thread's strand as its owner, and notices go to that owner through creel rather than to a fixed `ly:orch`.
- Threads talk to each other through creel posts, as strands already can.
- This builds on `orch-split` (a Go run driver beside a conversational agent): once the run loop is Go, a thread holds only the conversation and its own runs' escalations.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision: shared groundwork with Weaver

Umbrellas and `weaver` need the same primitive: create a pair from a parent pair's branch, merge it back into the parent, tear it down.
Today fabric creates a pair only from the worktree it runs in, and batten only from the prime.
That primitive is its own piece of groundwork, built before either umbrellas or Weaver.
Weaver's batches are not umbrellas: they are not board tasks, run as cold agents for minutes rather than loom runs for days, merge locally with Haiku resolving conflicts, and have no conversational thread.

## Folded in: a pair over an existing local branch (note `fabric-add-adopt-local`, 2026-10-22)

`lyx fabric add <slug>` adopts a warp branch that exists only on origin, or locally with the local-only mark, but refuses `ErrBranchExists` for an unmarked local branch (`internal/fabricengine/add.go`).
So there is no lyx way to make a pair over a branch already in this clone, such as `main` or a beam branch.
Case (orch, 2026-10-21): on the Models hub, as a stopgap until beams exist, the operator wanted the prime on a beam branch and `main` in its own worktree `main`; `lyx fabric add main` is refused, and would also fail on the weft side while `main-weft` is checked out in prime-weft.

Found in triage (2026-10-22), why it is not a small fix and waits for beams (operator agreed):

- `ErrBranchExists` is relied on: `internal/adoptcli` rewords it because dropping a leftover local branch loses unpushed commits, and `internal/battencli/wire.go` reads it to catch a leftover branch from a removed pair. Lifting the refusal for batten would let an unattended run adopt a stale branch for a new task of the same slug, so adoption of a local branch is allowed only when the operator runs `lyx fabric add` directly.
- `add` records the acting worktree's branch as the pair's parent, so `main` added from a prime on a beam branch would record the beam as `main`'s parent, the inverse of the truth, misleading every reader of that record (merge, landing).
- How a root pair is recorded (a pair over `main` or a beam branch, which batten never lands) is the beam design's own question; the prime being the root umbrella (above) answers it here.

The operator's view (2026-10-22): `add` is the verb that adopts an existing branch, local or remote, and a slug colliding with a leftover branch is the user's mistake; `fabric checkout` stays the verb that switches a worktree's branch.
A branch checked out in another worktree is refused with a message naming that worktree and `lyx fabric checkout` to move it off.

## Operator decision (2026-10-24): a VS Code workspace file per beam

- Each beam gets its own `<repo>-<beam>.code-workspace` directly in the hub folder, beside the hub's `<repo>.code-workspace`.
- Each file shows one level only. A beam's file lists the beam's own worktree, its parent's worktree (the prime or the parent beam it lands into), Bolt, the beam's own task worktrees, and for each sub-beam only that sub-beam's own worktree, since the sub-beam has its own file.
- It is written when the beam is created, kept current as its worktrees come and go, and removed when the beam lands.
- The hub's `<repo>.code-workspace` follows the same rule: the prime, Bolt, the task worktrees directly under `main`, and each top-level beam's own worktree, never the worktrees under a beam.

entries.title: Rename the Merge-In row to Parent-Align
entries.brief: The row aligns the task with what the parent brought in, not only merges
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-24)

Since `loom-tail-review` landed, loom's `Merge-In` row does more than merge: it takes the parent in, and when the parent brought commits in, or the merge conflicts or fails its gate, its fixer resolves the conflicts, makes the tests green and checks that the task's work still matches its decision record against what came in, escalating a decision that collides with landed work.
Without new parent commits and with a green gate it runs no fixer.
That second part is the old alignment check, moved in and narrowed to what the parent brought.
`Finalize` keeps its own small merge-in under the parent lock, as a last sync.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-24)

Rename the row `Merge-In` to `Parent-Align`, so its name says it aligns the task with its parent, not only merges.
The rename covers the recipe row in loom and darn, the producer and engine names, the `merge_*` config keys it reads, the stencils and docs.
Row names are durable resume identities, so a run parked on `Merge-In` is restarted, as the recipe already says for retired rows.

entries.title: A landing fixer escalation goes to the arbiter before the orch
entries.brief: Merge-In and Finalize fixer escalate reports reach the arbiter first
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-24)

A landing-stop halt at `Merge-In` or `Finalize`, the merge fixer's `escalate` report included, goes straight to the orch: `internal/arbiterstop` marks it `LandingHalt` and skips the arbiter, and `landingshed.HandsBack` names it a hand-back.
The fixer escalates when a decision in the task collides with work the parent brought in, the one case with a real judgement in it; the old alignment agent rejected 4 of 72 such checks, all valid.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-24)

A fixer's `escalate` at a landing row goes to the arbiter first, as other stops do: the arbiter is a strong agent that can likely settle a decision collision against the decision record and what landed, and only its hand-on reaches the orch.
A spent cap, a failed or unusable fixer turn and an over-cap change stay as they are.

entries.title: Find why a running run shows a dead waiter in the activity reader
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-24)

Task `idle-notice-no-live-run` landed as 450bc6ff1 with diagnostics only: `ReadAgentActivity` still skips a running run whose waiter pid is dead, so the idle notice can still say "no agent activity readable" while an agent works; it now logs that case (Warn once per episode). The root cause is unconfirmed.

## Idea

When the Warn line shows up in a run, read it with the run records and fix the cause: either the waiter pid recorded is wrong, or a live run legitimately has no waiter and the reader should read activity anyway.

entries.title: Plan conflict from a moved tree: a small fixer before the Plan perch
entries.brief: A tree_moved plan conflict naming exact glyphs goes to a small card fixer, not a full Plan review round
entries.body:
## Seen (gate-runs-once, 2026-10-24)

Batch 06's fork replaced `internal/gatecli#runGuardStep` with `guardStepRun`, as a deviation; its report warned that card 14 still named the old function.
`begin-batch 08` then refused with `plan_conflict: tree_moved` on card 14's glyph, and Webster's `on_reroute: Plan-Burler-Review` sent the run through a full Plan perch: Plan-Burler-Review, Plan-Burler-Fix and Plan-Bouncer, 11:45 to 12:01 local, before Webster resumed at batch 08.
The fix was one renamed glyph in one card, which the refusal named exactly.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-24)

A `tree_moved` conflict whose refusal names the missing glyphs and cards goes to a small fixer agent first, not to a full review perch: it edits the named cards to match the tree, runs `lyx webster rebaseline --card NN`, and Webster begins the batch again.
Only a conflict the fixer cannot settle, or one that changes a card's intent, goes on to Plan-Burler-Review.

entries.title: Plan check does not project the lint-pattern step per card, so a wrong plan-review fix passes review and fails only at self-check
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #866](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/866).

What happened: a plan-Burler fix moved a shortening card ahead of growth cards on the premise that each intermediate file size stays at or below the final projection.
A card gate does not apply that bound: once a file is above `HeadroomBytes`, a card's `lint-pattern` step passes only when the card does not grow the file.
The move required a `remove-card` plus `insert-card` that renumbered about twenty cards and needed every prose card reference fixed by hand; the self-check then showed the last growth card still failed, and undoing it took another `remove-card` and a second pass over the references.

Why abnormal: the plan check validates only the final size against the base, so neither the original defect nor the wrong fix was visible at the review stage, and card renumbering is costly to repeat.

What to do: make the plan check project `lint-pattern` card by card (the running size against the headroom rule), and consider renumbering helpers that update prose card references automatically.

Provenance: task gate-runs-once; notes burler-plan-r1.md

entries.title: Webster batch whose card verify needs an orch-only change dead-ends: recover-batch ends dead with 'asking', then the run halts repeatedly with growing history
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #867](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/867).

What happened: in batch 22 the fork reported stuck because a card's verify needed the hub's tier commands changed, which only the orch can do.
`lyx webster recover-batch 22` ended dead with dead_reason asking and recovery_retry false, and the refusal said to end the run stuck.
A second refusal record for the same batch shows dead_reason died, recoveries 1 and recovery_retry true, with the way forward 'run recover-batch 22 once more'.
The run then halted blocked (anomaly escalation-to-human) three times; each re-entry appended further Webster stuck entries to the history, and the later halts said the recovery was exhausted and that later batches were not begun.
Separately, a begin-batch refusal reported plan_conflict tree_moved for a card target whose unit exists but whose member is missing, with the way forward being rebaseline.

Why abnormal: a need that only the orch can satisfy is classified as a dead recovery instead of a request to the parent, so the recovery budget is spent and the run can only halt for a human; the two refusals for one batch give contradictory recovery_retry and dead_reason values, and repeated re-entry of a halted run adds stuck history without progress.

What to do: let a fork's 'needs orch action' report route to the parent (a message or a distinct pause state) without consuming the recovery budget, keep recovery_retry and dead_reason consistent across consecutive recover-batch refusals, and make a re-entry of an already-halted escalation return the existing halt rather than append another stuck entry.

Provenance: task gate-runs-once; notes loom-halt.md, loom-halt-2.md, loom-halt-3.md, webster-refusal-recover-batch.md, webster-refusal-recover-batch-2.md, webster-refusal-begin-batch.md

## Design choice (operator left it to the orch, 2026-10-24)

A fork's "needs orch action" report puts Webster into a waiting state of its own that spends no recovery budget, and the orch is told; once the orch has acted, the batch resumes where it stood.
No distinct halt type is added.
